events.excerpt: Hi all, I’ve submitted a ZCG grant application and I’m posting it here for community input, as required: Grant Application - PrivateSync: Privacy-Preserving Light Client Sync Infrastructure for Zcash · Issue #549 · ZcashCommunityGrants/zcashcommunitygrants · GitHub The problem: Zashi/Ywallet sync through lightwalletd servers, and that sync leaks the user’s IP address and which compact blocks the wallet downloads — a metadata trail that can deanonymize otherwise shielded activity. lightwalletd’s own wallet-app threat model documents these limitations, and ZCG’s open RFP for lightwalletd infrastructure asks for a multi-operator solution. The proposal: a three-tier privacy stack for light client sync, aligned with upstream work already in flight (librustzcash #2665 , SDK #1741 ): Tier 1 — Tor onion sync for lightwalletd (ships first) Tier 2 — Tor + multi-server PIR, where no single sync node learns which block you requested (information-theoretic, per-server privacy) Deployment: 3–5 independently operated testnet nodes + a runbook so more operators can join — the multi-team model the RFP calls for Ask: $27,000 over 8 months, paid per milestone, no upfront. Evidence base (everything is public): Application repo (proposal, whitepaper, budget, verified research): GitHub - sarinsk629-bl
events.headline: ZCG Application — PrivateSync: Privacy-Preserving Light Client Sync Infrastructure (feedback wanted)

events.excerpt: When a module limits what governance can do with it, a cap on what a treasury pays out per week or a list of addresses a reserve is allowed to pay, the easy place for that limit is the module’s params. The authority for MsgUpdateParams is then the same gov account the limit is meant to hold back. That came up in the Luggom thread here in October, and the fix was in their repo the same day. I think it’s general enough for its own topic, because it’s easy to miss when you read the module on its own. What x/gov does when a proposal passes In SDK v0.53.8, the version Gaia v29 runs, the gov EndBlocker tallies the vote and, if it passed, opens one cached context and runs the proposal’s messages in the order they were submitted ( abci.go L166-L217 ). Every message sees what the ones before it wrote. If one fails, nothing is written and the proposal is marked failed. So a proposal with a MsgUpdateParams that adds a payee or raises the cap, followed by the spend, passes the module’s check in the same block. Nothing runs before the vote either. At submission SubmitProposal runs each message’s ValidateBasic , checks that its only signer is the gov account and that the router knows the type ( proposal.go L46-L69 ), and that’s it. Voters do see both messages, if they open the proposal and rea
events.headline: One proposal can lift a module's limit and use it in the same block

events.excerpt: This proposal specifies the JSON document that tokenURI returns in ERC-721 and ERC-6909 and that uri returns in ERC-1155 . Most deployed tokens already use this format, but only part of it was ever specified. ERC-721 and ERC-1155 define name , description and image . Everything else wallets and marketplaces show ( animation_url , attributes and its display_type values, external_url , background_color ) comes from a page OpenSea published in 2018. Clients fill the gaps differently, so the same token renders differently from one app to the next. Draft: erc-8495.md ( ethereum/ERCs#2163 ) The draft covers: Every field and its type, every display_type value in use, and what clients do with values that don’t match, such as booleans, quoted numbers and dates in milliseconds. The URI schemes clients must resolve ( https , ipfs , ar , data ), the ones they may resolve ( ipns , and web3 from ERC-4804 ), and the ones they must never resolve. events.excerpt: Hi all — EnsRationis from Robonomics. Sensors.social is an open environmental data network I designed, and it is now growing across the EU. Everything is open source: the Altruist sensors that feed it, the software that collects the readings, and the map. Web3 does one job here, the one it is good at: it settles the data as a common good anyone can check, not a vendor’s database. How it works on Robonomics Owners who choose to share their Altruist’s data join the network; each sensor has its own key and signs every measurement it sends. A connectivity node checks the signature and that the sensor has an active subscription on Robonomics, a parachain on Polkadot, then passes the reading to the live map. The node collects readings into batches, stores each batch on IPFS and writes its hash to Robonomics. Anyone can fetch a batch and check it against the chain. The network is federated: a city or a lab can run its own connectivity node, and its sensors still show up on the common map. Next, with Robonomics 5.0: the reading the sensor signed goes on chain itself, so there is no need to trust the node at all. Try the map: https://sensors.social Happy to hear from anyone who wants to run a sensor in their city or build on the data. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic
events.headline: Sensors.social: an open air-quality network on Polkadot is growing across the EU

Specification Draft PR #2159 Problem and scope A payment institution needs to distinguish a customer’s business entries from changes to the spending capacity it grants. It also needs to connect individual entries, current-period totals, and sealed periods when reconciling customer funds. An institution-level aggregate does not provide those per-account records. This proposal defines a common contract interface for those records and controls. It can serve an institution’s own business independently or compose with an on-chain payment protocol. It does not issue or transfer assets, establish customer identity, or prove that funds have been frozen or settled. Account model and interface Each account is scoped by (account, institution) . An institution can serve payer accounts, merchant accounts, or both; the same address at two institutions does not share records or capacity. Holding the account’s private key does not grant permission to write entries. events.excerpt: Hi everyone, AI agents now take on paid work on-chain. The client locks the pay in an escrow, and the escrow pays the agent when the work is accepted. As this grows, each payment also has to cover others: a tax that funds public services, a fee to whoever referred the job, or the repayment of a loan the agent took to do the job. This is a draft ERC for Settlement Deductions . It lets an escrow withhold these amounts from each payout. The escrow does not need to know the rules behind them. None of them can stall the payout. It works for any task escrow, not only those used by agents. Example: a payout of 100, with a 1% tax, a 2% referral fee and a repayment of 30. The treasury gets 1, the referrer 2, the lender 30. The payee gets 67. I will open the PR to ethereum/ERCs next, with this thread as its discussion link. The slot this fills Escrows for agent work end in one transfer to the payee. events.excerpt: This is the discussion thread for EIP-8487 (PR: Add EIP: Separate execution credits and billing credits by Giulio2002 · Pull Request #12637 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub ). The proposal introduces two counters, both initialized from tx.gasLimit : Credits follow the legacy gas schedule and are the only gas the EVM sees (GAS opcode, call forwarding, creation). Billing follows the new schedule and determines the transaction fee. If billing runs out, the whole transaction aborts (uncatchable), even if credits remain. The goal is to let opcodes be repriced without changing execution behavior for contracts that inspect or forward gas. Open questions: the exact schedules, charge points, rebate rules, receipt fields and block accounting. Feedback welcome. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full topic

events.excerpt: The verified badge on an explorer shows that some source compiles to the code at an address. It doesn’t say which commit that source came from, and on a proxy it says nothing about the logic behind it. So when someone asks whether an upgradeable contract still runs the commit its audit covered, the honest answer is often a guess, and a few upgrades after launch the guess can be wrong. I’ve been writing down what a real check needs. Most of it is small. Rebuilding the commit To tie the address to the report you rebuild the audited commit with the same settings (solc version, optimizer runs, viaIR, evmVersion) and compare runtime bytecode. If the contract has immutables, it won’t match byte for byte. The constructor writes their values into the runtime code, so a fresh build has zeros where the deployed code has an oracle address or a fee. solc gives you the positions in evm.deployedBytecode.immutableReferences in the standard JSON output. Zero those ranges on the deployed side, compare, and then check the immutable values on their own. What this basically means is that a clean build with the wrong oracle baked in still passes the bytecode comparison. The end of the bytecode is the other place it breaks. solc appends the IPFS hash of the metadata file, and the metadata holds a hash
events.headline: Checking that a deployed contract still runs the audited commit

events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX)
events.headline: Per-Asset Liquidation Thresholds Underpredict Co-Liquidation by 301×

events.excerpt: AAVE SECURITY SHIELD Propuesta comunitaria para reforzar la prevención de riesgos externos y la protección de los depositantes Tipo: Iniciativa comunitaria para discusión y evaluación preliminar Área: Seguridad, gestión de riesgos y resiliencia financiera Estado: Borrador conceptual previo a una posible ARFC Autoría: Iniciativa comunitaria independiente Solicitud inicial: Evaluar el interés de la comunidad en financiar o realizar un estudio de viabilidad, sin aprobar todavía modificaciones del protocolo. PARTE I. PRESENTACIÓN DE LA INICIATIVA 1. Resumen ejecutivo La pregunta que queremos plantear a la comunidad de Aave es: ¿Cómo puede Aave limitar la generación de nueva exposición crediticia durante un incidente de seguridad externo, sin perjudicar innecesariamente a sus usuarios? AAVE SECURITY SHIELD es una iniciativa comunitaria que propone estudiar una capa adicional de prevención, complementaria a los mecanismos de seguridad, gestión de riesgos y respuesta a emergencias existentes en el protocolo. El objetivo es investigar si determinados controles pueden proporcionar a Aave más tiempo para verificar una amenaza y contener su impacto antes de que se acumule una exposición significativa. La iniciativa propone evaluar mecanismos que permitan: Identificar amenazas externas media
events.headline: [TEMP CHECK] AAVE SECURITY SHIELD – Exploring Preventive Risk Controls for External Security Incidents

events.excerpt: Status: filed as ethereum/ERCs pull request #2155 ; number ERC-8490 assigned on 2026-11-09. Reference repository: GitHub - garyyang-finchip/agent-meditation-mechanism: Agent Meditation Mechanism · GitHub . Sepolia evidence: recorded in the repository and summarized in a reply below. This draft proposes a minimal registry through which an AI agent records its own self-maintenance: what it checked, cleaned, repaired, updated and reconsidered about itself, as a versioned and attributable history. The name follows the human analogy of maintenance that happens in a quiet phase (sleep, meditation); the mechanism itself is deliberately dry. Why a registry at all. An agent keeps its identity while its code, dependencies, memories, skills, plans and ways of judging keep changing. Agent runtimes already do this maintenance in the background (self-checks, dependency walks, memory consolidation, re-planning, reflection), and the results stay local. Nothing connects the successive states of one agent into a history another party can recognize, and nothing lets a counterparty ask: which state is registered now, which layers were checked recently and which of them changed, under which rules in effect at the time, and did the cycle adopt an update, confirm that nothing needed to change, or fail?
events.headline: ERC-8490: Agent Meditation Mechanism

events.excerpt: Summary. AIFP is a framework ERC for the information layer between agents. It defines a flow paradigm as a content-addressed, versioned description of an interaction context - which carriers (addressed delivery, shared object) and structural operators (fan-out, fan-in, feedback, n-party, select, forward, derive, merge) it uses, and how thirteen separately declared rule dimensions are set (discovery, observation, contribution, management, redistribution, history, time, disclosure timing, contributor visibility, admission basis, representation, object relations, ordering). A channel adopts exactly one paradigm version at any timepoint. Participation is recorded as separately addressable role bindings with a scope, a basis, a validity interval and the rule version they were granted under. Role acquisition is checked by composable predicates that answer one of four outcomes: satisfied, not satisfied, undeterminable, verifier error. Status. Draft. Filed as ethereum/ERCs PR #2152 ; the editors assigned the number ERC-8489 on 2026-11-09 ( ERCS/erc-8489.md , assets under assets/erc-8489/ ). Reference repository with the Foundry suite, the canonical validator and the vectors: garyyang-finchip/aif-paradigm . The reference stack is deployed on Sepolia and the boundary-case evidence run is r

events.excerpt: TL;DR: An opt-in, public, per-account “protected” flag for ERC-20s. Small sends stay instant; anything bigger is scheduled and can be cancelled by a pre-registered backup wallet; a “stress” action sweeps everything to the backup and locks it, which also helps against wrench attacks. Turning protection on is instant; weakening it (off, higher limit, shorter waits, new backup) takes a delay the holder picks. Why: Today a stolen key or a coerced holder means an instant, final drain. Existing approaches are per-transfer (SLOW), need recipient cooperation (ERC-8236), need judges (ERC-20R), protect protocols rather than users (ERC-7265), or only work in one smart wallet. This puts the protection in the token, so it works for any holder and any wallet, including plain EOAs. How it works: protect(backup, dailyLimit, holdWindow, offDelay, lockDuration, fastLane) : instant. Over-limit transferFrom reverts (never returns true without moving tokens, so routers, vaults and lenders can’t be fooled). Over-limit transfer from an EOA may be auto-scheduled, so wallet “Send” buttons just work. queueTransfer → hold window → anyone can executeTransfer ; the owner or backup can cancelTransfer ; with the opt-in fast lane, the backup can approveTransfer to skip the wait. stress(account) : cancels everyt
